title: Large-Scale AI Training & Inference
blurb: DDP, FSDP/ZeRO, tensor/pipeline/context/expert parallelism, mixed precision, checkpoints, inference engines, batching and benchmarking.
description: A systems-focused AI scaling course aligned to NVIDIA DLI distributed-training and accelerated-inference curricula and modern PyTorch distributed practice.

lessons.title: Why AI workloads stop fitting on one device
objectives: Diagnose whether a workload is limited by model memory, activations, compute, data, or communication.
Explain how scaling bottleneck changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect scaling bottleneck with memory and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Large-scale AI starts with resource accounting. Model parameters, optimizer states, gradients, activations, KV cache, input batches, and temporary buffers all consume memory; training also requires much more compute and communication than inference.
lessons.explain: Large-scale AI starts with resource accounting. Model parameters, optimizer states, gradients, activations, KV cache, input batches, and temporary buffers all consume memory; training also requires much more compute and communication than inference.
examples:
gb={"parameters":28,"optimizer":56,"gradients":28,"activations":20}
print("estimated training memory",sum(gb.values()),"GB")
lessons.example:
gb={"parameters":28,"optimizer":56,"gradients":28,"activations":20}
print("estimated training memory",sum(gb.values()),"GB")
commonMistakes: Adding more GPUs without identifying the bottleneck can increase communication overhead while leaving data loading or a serial stage unchanged.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: GPU topology, memory hierarchy & bandwidth
objectives: Explain why device placement and interconnect topology affect scaling performance.
Explain how GPU memory changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect GPU memory with PCIe and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Accelerators have fast local memory and arithmetic, but data movement through HBM, PCIe, NVLink, NICs, and host memory has different bandwidth and latency. Multi-GPU performance depends on which devices communicate and how they are connected.
lessons.explain: Accelerators have fast local memory and arithmetic, but data movement through HBM, PCIe, NVLink, NICs, and host memory has different bandwidth and latency. Multi-GPU performance depends on which devices communicate and how they are connected.
lessons.example:
links={"HBM":"very high","NVLink":"high","PCIe":"lower","network":"cluster dependent"}
for k,v in links.items(): print(k,v)
commonMistakes: Assuming every pair of GPUs communicates at the same speed can produce severe imbalance on multi-socket or multi-node systems.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Data parallelism & PyTorch DDP
objectives: Scale training by replicating the model and splitting each global batch across workers.
Explain how data parallelism changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data parallelism with DDP and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data parallelism gives each worker a model replica, processes different samples, and synchronizes gradients before the optimizer step. PyTorch DistributedDataParallel overlaps gradient all-reduce with backpropagation and is the standard baseline for multi-GPU training when the model fits on each device.
lessons.explain: Data parallelism gives each worker a model replica, processes different samples, and synchronizes gradients before the optimizer step. PyTorch DistributedDataParallel overlaps gradient all-reduce with backpropagation and is the standard baseline for multi-GPU training when the model fits on each device.
examples:
world_size=8
per_gpu=4
accumulation=2
print("global batch",world_size*per_gpu*accumulation)
lessons.example:
world_size=8; per_gpu=4; accumulation=2
print("global batch",world_size*per_gpu*accumulation)
commonMistakes: Increasing world size while accidentally increasing global batch size can change optimization behavior, so a speed comparison may no longer be apples-to-apples.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Collective communication & synchronization
objectives: Understand the communication primitives behind distributed training.
Explain how all-reduce changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect all-reduce with all-gather and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Distributed training composes a few collective operations. All-reduce combines values such as gradients across workers; all-gather collects sharded tensors; reduce-scatter combines and redistributes pieces.
lessons.explain: Distributed training composes a few collective operations. All-reduce combines values such as gradients across workers; all-gather collects sharded tensors; reduce-scatter combines and redistributes pieces.
examples:
workers=[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]
summed=[sum(x) for x in zip(*workers)]
print("all-reduce conceptual sum",summed)
lessons.example:
workers=[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]
summed=[sum(x) for x in zip(*workers)]
print("all-reduce conceptual sum",summed)
commonMistakes: Adding frequent synchronization inside small operations can make communication latency dominate even when total data volume is not large.

lessons.title: FSDP / ZeRO-style parameter sharding
objectives: Train models that do not fit as full replicas on every GPU.
Explain how FSDP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect FSDP with ZeRO and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Fully sharded approaches partition model parameters, gradients, and/or optimizer states across workers instead of storing complete copies everywhere. Parameters can be gathered just in time for computation and released or reshared afterward.
lessons.explain: Fully sharded approaches partition model parameters, gradients, and/or optimizer states across workers instead of storing complete copies everywhere. Parameters can be gathered just in time for computation and released or reshared afterward.
examples:
model_gb=80
workers=8
print("idealized parameter shard",model_gb/workers,"GB per worker before overhead")
lessons.example:
model_gb=80; workers=8
print("idealized parameter shard",model_gb/workers,"GB per worker before overhead")
commonMistakes: Assuming memory divides perfectly by world size ignores activations, temporary all-gathers, fragmentation, buffers, and uneven module sizes.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Tensor parallelism
objectives: Split the computation of large layers across devices.
Explain how tensor parallelism changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tensor parallelism with sharded matmul and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tensor parallelism partitions weight matrices or attention/MLP dimensions so several GPUs cooperate on one layer. Each device computes a shard and exchanges partial results through collectives.
lessons.explain: Tensor parallelism partitions weight matrices or attention/MLP dimensions so several GPUs cooperate on one layer. Each device computes a shard and exchanges partial results through collectives.
examples:
hidden=8192
tp=8
print("hidden features per idealized shard",hidden//tp)
lessons.example:
hidden=8192; tp=8
print("hidden features per idealized shard",hidden//tp)
commonMistakes: Using tensor parallelism across slow network boundaries can spend more time exchanging partial activations than performing matrix multiplications.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Pipeline parallelism & microbatches
objectives: Split model layers into stages and keep them busy with microbatches.
Explain how pipeline parallelism changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pipeline parallelism with microbatch and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Pipeline parallelism places different layer ranges on different devices. Microbatches flow through stages like an assembly line so several batches can be in flight.
lessons.explain: Pipeline parallelism places different layer ranges on different devices. Microbatches flow through stages like an assembly line so several batches can be in flight.
examples:
stage_ms=[12,12,25,11]
print("bottleneck stage ms",max(stage_ms))
lessons.example:
stage_ms=[12,12,25,11]
print("bottleneck stage ms",max(stage_ms))
commonMistakes: Splitting layers evenly by count can produce badly imbalanced stages because layers differ in compute and memory cost.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Sequence/context parallelism for long inputs
objectives: Partition long-sequence computation and activations across devices.
Explain how sequence parallelism changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect sequence parallelism with context parallelism and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Long-context workloads can be activation- and attention-memory heavy even when parameters fit. Sequence/context parallel techniques partition token dimensions or attention computation so multiple devices share the work.
lessons.explain: Long-context workloads can be activation- and attention-memory heavy even when parameters fit. Sequence/context parallel techniques partition token dimensions or attention computation so multiple devices share the work.
examples:
tokens=128000
workers=8
print("tokens per idealized context shard",tokens//workers)
lessons.example:
tokens=128000; workers=8
print("tokens per idealized context shard",tokens//workers)
commonMistakes: Only sharding parameters does not solve activation and attention-memory growth caused by very long sequences.

lessons.title: Expert parallelism & mixture-of-experts
objectives: Understand sparse expert routing and why load balancing becomes a systems problem.
Explain how MoE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MoE with expert parallelism and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a subset of expert networks for each token. Expert parallelism distributes experts across devices and routes token representations to the selected experts.
lessons.explain: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a subset of expert networks for each token. Expert parallelism distributes experts across devices and routes token representations to the selected experts.
examples:
routes=[0,0,1,3,0,2,3,3]
from collections import Counter
print(Counter(routes))
lessons.example:
routes=[0,0,1,3,0,2,3,3]
from collections import Counter
print(Counter(routes))
commonMistakes: A router that sends too many tokens to a few experts creates hotspots and can waste the theoretical efficiency of sparse computation.

lessons.title: Mixed precision: FP32, BF16, FP16 & loss scaling
objectives: Reduce memory and accelerate tensor-core compute without losing numerical stability.
Explain how mixed precision changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect mixed precision with BF16 and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Mixed-precision training stores or computes many tensors in lower precision while preserving sensitive operations or master states as needed. BF16 has a wide exponent range and is often easier to train with than FP16; FP16 may require dynamic loss scaling to avoid gradient underflow.
lessons.explain: Mixed-precision training stores or computes many tensors in lower precision while preserving sensitive operations or master states as needed. BF16 has a wide exponent range and is often easier to train with than FP16; FP16 may require dynamic loss scaling to avoid gradient underflow.
lessons.example:
bytes_per_param={"fp32":4,"bf16":2,"fp16":2,"int8":1}
for p,b in bytes_per_param.items(): print(p,b)
commonMistakes: A run that is faster but silently diverges or changes model quality is not a successful mixed-precision optimization.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Gradient accumulation & effective batch size
objectives: Reach a larger effective batch when a full batch cannot fit in memory.
Explain how gradient accumulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect gradient accumulation with microbatch and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Gradient accumulation performs several forward/backward microbatches before the optimizer step. It reduces peak activation memory relative to one large batch and can emulate a larger global batch, but it increases step latency and changes how often optimizer schedules advance.
lessons.explain: Gradient accumulation performs several forward/backward microbatches before the optimizer step. It reduces peak activation memory relative to one large batch and can emulate a larger global batch, but it increases step latency and changes how often optimizer schedules advance.
examples:
micro=2
accumulation=16
dp=8
print("effective batch",micro*accumulation*dp)
lessons.example:
micro=2; accumulation=16; dp=8
print("effective batch",micro*accumulation*dp)
commonMistakes: Dividing loss incorrectly or stepping the optimizer on every microbatch changes the optimization problem instead of merely accumulating gradients.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Activation checkpointing / recomputation
objectives: Trade extra compute for lower activation memory.
Explain how activation checkpointing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect activation checkpointing with recomputation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Backpropagation normally needs intermediate activations from the forward pass. Activation checkpointing saves selected checkpoints and recomputes missing intermediates during backward, lowering memory usage at the cost of additional compute.
lessons.explain: Backpropagation normally needs intermediate activations from the forward pass. Activation checkpointing saves selected checkpoints and recomputes missing intermediates during backward, lowering memory usage at the cost of additional compute.
examples:
layers=48
checkpoints=8
print("layers per checkpoint region",layers//checkpoints)
lessons.example:
layers=48; checkpoints=8
print("layers per checkpoint region",layers//checkpoints)
commonMistakes: Checkpointing every tiny operation may save memory but add so much recomputation and framework overhead that training slows dramatically.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Distributed data loading & input pipelines
objectives: Feed accelerators fast enough without duplicating or skipping training data.
Explain how data sharding changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data sharding with sampler and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every data-parallel worker should process an appropriate shard of the dataset while maintaining the intended randomness and epoch semantics. Input decoding, tokenization, augmentation, storage bandwidth, worker count, prefetching, and host-to-device transfer can all starve GPUs.
lessons.explain: Every data-parallel worker should process an appropriate shard of the dataset while maintaining the intended randomness and epoch semantics. Input decoding, tokenization, augmentation, storage bandwidth, worker count, prefetching, and host-to-device transfer can all starve GPUs.
examples:
indices=list(range(20))
rank=2
world=4
print("rank shard",indices[rank::world])
lessons.example:
indices=list(range(20)); rank=2; world=4
print("rank shard",indices[rank::world])
commonMistakes: Letting every worker iterate the complete dataset without a distributed sampler duplicates examples and changes the effective training distribution.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Distributed checkpoints & resuming jobs
objectives: Save model, optimizer, scheduler, RNG, and data position so a large job can resume correctly.
Explain how checkpoint changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect checkpoint with state dict and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A useful training checkpoint includes enough state to continue the same optimization process: model parameters, optimizer state, scheduler/scaler, random-number state, global step, and often data-loader progress. Sharded training may use distributed checkpoint formats to avoid gathering the full model on one host.
lessons.explain: A useful training checkpoint includes enough state to continue the same optimization process: model parameters, optimizer state, scheduler/scaler, random-number state, global step, and often data-loader progress. Sharded training may use distributed checkpoint formats to avoid gathering the full model on one host.
examples:
checkpoint={"step":12000,"model":"sharded","optimizer":"sharded","rng":"saved"}
print(checkpoint)
lessons.example:
checkpoint={"step":12000,"model":"sharded","optimizer":"sharded","rng":"saved"}
print(checkpoint)
commonMistakes: Saving only model weights allows inference but does not reproduce a true training resume because optimizer and scheduler state are missing.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Fault tolerance, preemption & elastic recovery
objectives: Design long-running training jobs to survive expected infrastructure failures.
Explain how fault tolerance changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect fault tolerance with preemption and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Large distributed jobs have a larger failure surface: any worker, node, storage path, or network link can fail. Periodic checkpoints, idempotent launch scripts, retry policies, health monitoring, and preemption-aware scheduling reduce lost work.
lessons.explain: Large distributed jobs have a larger failure surface: any worker, node, storage path, or network link can fail. Periodic checkpoints, idempotent launch scripts, retry policies, health monitoring, and preemption-aware scheduling reduce lost work.
examples:
hours_per_ckpt=1
job_hours=200
print("maximum compute lost after one failure about",hours_per_ckpt,"hour")
lessons.example:
hours_per_ckpt=1; job_hours=200
print("maximum compute lost after one failure about",hours_per_ckpt,"hour")
commonMistakes: Checkpointing only once a day on an expensive preemptible cluster can turn an ordinary node failure into many hours of lost compute.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Profiling distributed training & utilization
objectives: Measure where distributed time is spent and optimize the dominant bottleneck.
Explain how profiling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect profiling with MFU and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Distributed profiling separates useful accelerator compute from input wait, communication, synchronization, kernel launch overhead, memory stalls, and idle pipeline time. GPU utilization alone can be misleading because a device may be busy with inefficient operations.
lessons.explain: Distributed profiling separates useful accelerator compute from input wait, communication, synchronization, kernel launch overhead, memory stalls, and idle pipeline time. GPU utilization alone can be misleading because a device may be busy with inefficient operations.
examples:
single=100
eight_gpu=610
print("speedup",eight_gpu/single,"efficiency",(eight_gpu/single)/8)
lessons.example:
single=100; eight_gpu=610
print("speedup",eight_gpu/single,"efficiency",(eight_gpu/single)/8)
commonMistakes: Calling an 8-GPU run “8× scaled” without comparing throughput against the single-GPU baseline hides poor scaling efficiency.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Inference memory: weights, activations & serving state
objectives: Account for model weights, temporary activations, runtime buffers, and concurrent requests.
Explain how inference memory changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect inference memory with serving and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Inference removes optimizer and training-gradient memory, but serving adds concurrency and request-specific state. Weight precision determines static model memory; activations and workspace depend on batch and sequence shapes; autoregressive LLMs add KV cache that grows with active tokens.
lessons.explain: Inference removes optimizer and training-gradient memory, but serving adds concurrency and request-specific state. Weight precision determines static model memory; activations and workspace depend on batch and sequence shapes; autoregressive LLMs add KV cache that grows with active tokens.
examples:
budget={"weights":28,"kv_cache":18,"workspace":6,"headroom":8}
print("serving memory budget",sum(budget.values()),"GB")
lessons.example:
budget={"weights":28,"kv_cache":18,"workspace":6,"headroom":8}
print("serving memory budget",sum(budget.values()),"GB")
commonMistakes: Testing only one short prompt at a time does not prove the model will fit under concurrent long-context production traffic.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: KV cache & long-context serving
objectives: Explain how KV caching speeds autoregressive generation and why it consumes serving memory.
Explain how KV cache changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect KV cache with attention and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Autoregressive transformers reuse keys and values from previous tokens instead of recomputing the full prefix at every generation step. The KV cache makes decoding much faster but grows with active sequence length, layer count, head dimensions, batch/concurrency, and cache precision.
lessons.explain: Autoregressive transformers reuse keys and values from previous tokens instead of recomputing the full prefix at every generation step. The KV cache makes decoding much faster but grows with active sequence length, layer count, head dimensions, batch/concurrency, and cache precision.
examples:
requests={"short":1000,"long":64000}
print("long context is",requests["long"]//requests["short"],"x tokens")
lessons.example:
requests={"short":1000,"long":64000}
print("long context is",requests["long"]//requests["short"],"x tokens")
commonMistakes: Sizing a server by weight memory alone can leave no room for KV cache once several long requests become active.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Batching & continuous batching
objectives: Increase accelerator utilization while controlling per-request latency.
Explain how batching changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect batching with continuous batching and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Static batching waits to form a group of requests and processes them together, improving throughput but potentially increasing queue delay. Autoregressive requests finish at different times, so continuous batching admits new work as slots become available instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish.
lessons.explain: Static batching waits to form a group of requests and processes them together, improving throughput but potentially increasing queue delay. Autoregressive requests finish at different times, so continuous batching admits new work as slots become available instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish.
examples:
arrival_ms=[0,4,8,30]
batch_window=10
first_batch=[t for t in arrival_ms if t<=batch_window]
print(first_batch)
lessons.example:
arrival_ms=[0,4,8,30]; batch_window=10
first_batch=[t for t in arrival_ms if t<=batch_window]
print(first_batch)
commonMistakes: Maximizing batch size without a latency SLO can improve tokens/sec while making individual users wait unacceptably long.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Quantization, sharding & speculative decoding
objectives: Compare complementary methods for reducing memory or decoding cost.
Explain how quantization changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect quantization with inference sharding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Quantization stores or computes weights/activations with fewer bits to reduce memory bandwidth and capacity requirements, with possible quality or kernel trade-offs. Inference sharding distributes a model that is too large or latency-sensitive for one device.
lessons.explain: Quantization stores or computes weights/activations with fewer bits to reduce memory bandwidth and capacity requirements, with possible quality or kernel trade-offs. Inference sharding distributes a model that is too large or latency-sensitive for one device.
lessons.example:
params_b=70
for bits in [16,8,4]: print(bits,"bit ideal weight GB",params_b*bits/8)
commonMistakes: Choosing 4-bit quantization solely from memory savings without evaluating task quality and runtime kernel support can produce a slower or less accurate deployment.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Inference runtimes: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM & serving engines
objectives: Understand what specialized runtimes optimize beyond a plain model.forward loop.
Explain how inference runtime changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect inference runtime with vLLM and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Production inference engines coordinate memory management, optimized kernels, batching/scheduling, model parallelism, quantization, cache handling, and request APIs. Engines such as vLLM and TensorRT-LLM make different hardware and deployment trade-offs, so benchmarking on the target model and request distribution is more useful than choosing by reputation.
lessons.explain: Production inference engines coordinate memory management, optimized kernels, batching/scheduling, model parallelism, quantization, cache handling, and request APIs. Engines such as vLLM and TensorRT-LLM make different hardware and deployment trade-offs, so benchmarking on the target model and request distribution is more useful than choosing by reputation.
examples:
engines={"baseline":"framework eager","engine_A":"paged cache + continuous batching","engine_B":"compiled optimized kernels"}
print(engines)
lessons.example:
engines={"baseline":"framework eager","engine_A":"paged cache + continuous batching","engine_B":"compiled optimized kernels"}
print(engines)
commonMistakes: Comparing runtimes with different batch sizes, precision, context lengths, or output-token limits can create misleading benchmark conclusions.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Serving topology, autoscaling & inference benchmarking
objectives: Design and measure an inference service under realistic traffic.
Explain how autoscaling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect autoscaling with SLO and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A production topology includes routing, replicas, model workers, queues, health checks, autoscaling signals, observability, and failure handling. Benchmark both prefill and decode behavior across realistic prompt/output lengths and concurrency.
lessons.explain: A production topology includes routing, replicas, model workers, queues, health checks, autoscaling signals, observability, and failure handling. Benchmark both prefill and decode behavior across realistic prompt/output lengths and concurrency.
examples:
report={"p50_ms":180,"p95_ms":520,"tokens_per_s":9200,"error_rate":0.001,"concurrency":64}
print(report)
lessons.example:
report={"p50_ms":180,"p95_ms":520,"tokens_per_s":9200,"error_rate":0.001,"concurrency":64}
print(report)
commonMistakes: A single-request latency benchmark cannot predict throughput, queueing, or memory behavior under real concurrent traffic.
